title: Arrival story of Matteo Readelli (ESC volunteer from Italy)

data.text: The flight was definitely smoother than I had expected especially given the fact that I had only finished packing a few hours before taking off from Milano Malpensa airport. The flight lasted two and half hours and due to the time zone we lost an hour making it three. (CET to EET).
When we arrived in Kyiv the city lights illuminated the city from the darkness that surrounded Boryspil airport.
Photo by Anna Mangiullo

As soon as I stepped outside from the main hall of the airport the famous and most feared Ukrainian weather struck me to my bones. The temperature was around minus four degrees but surprisingly tolerable due to the low humidity. Who would believe that in Italy the weather conditions were worse than in Ukraine. Especially during the Italian winter when the temperature falls to three or four degrees with a high percentage of humidity. Italian humidity penetrates your bones and makes you run with haste towards warmth. However, after the first step on Ukrainian soil I thought I could easily bear the Ukrainian weather but to my shock the worst is yet to come. People from Pangeya Ultima ensured me that December is only the beginning and not the worst month of the year because Ukrainian temperatures during the last days of January and February usually reach -20°.

Upon meeting Zhenya, a former member of association, we reached the central station in Kyiv, ate something at Posata Xata (delicious!) and boarded our train heading towards Vinnytsia. The train was something I certainly did not expect. What at first impressed me the most was definitely the height of the train, I had two heavy suitcases with me and it was a difficult task to load them onto the train. After climbing the stairs of the train, I finally managed to get into the wagon and started looking for my seat. The problem was that there were no seats but only beds, Anna turned to me and said welcome to Ukraine traveling, platzkart style. In western Europe we do not have such things at all, the only night trains are rare and expensive.

Therefore, I did not expect a similar train at all here in Ukraine. For those who are reading and do not know what a plazkart train is, do not feel ignorant, I didn’t know either before coming to Ukraine. Platzkarts are eastern European trains wherein every five/six squared meters (yes, I tried to measure that space) are placed with six beds two stories high. The whole train was made out of glazed steel and wood with really few plastic components, which created a nicely old fashioned traveling environment. Furthermore, the train cabin crew provided every passenger with a pillow, bed linens, and a blanket. This was one of my biggest culture shocks of my arrival. During the journey to Vinnytsia I just remained seated upon my bed without even trying to sleep. However, next time I take the platzkart I will definitely try to sleep like a real Ukrainian.

After two and half hours of traveling we finally reached Vinnytsia where Iarik was waiting to pick us up. It was already 3 AM as we drove along Soborna street until reaching our accommodation. I even found a small cat, who became my first friend in Ukraine, before climbing the stairs and falling asleep on my bed after a long day of traveling. It was only the following morning that I saw the Ukrainian urban landscape around me from my windows with the huge brutal palaces, chimneys, and rich green areas. Now I can’t wait until spring when the neighborhood will spring to life with all the charms of summertime happiness.
#pangeyaESC
“Anna, but why Ukraine?”, Anna’s answer.

Ok so here I am in Ukraine, sitting in front of the window with a view of grey soviet buildings and leafless trees, writing the story of how I arrived here. I am not going to go into depth about how I traveled here. (if you want to know how I reached Vinnytsia you can just take a look to Matteo's story, since we traveled together). Instead I will share my pre-departure feelings and the reasons why I am volunteering in Vinnytsia.

Let’s start from the beginning: Hi, my name is Anna and last summer while I was writing my master thesis in Russian literature I decided I wanted a new experience for my life. After two months stuck in my little room in Italy, my only desire was to escape, travel, live as we once did and as soon as possible. As the ghost of winter lockdown was once again the knocking at the door. I immediately started checking the ESC website for my way to escape. I already heard of these ESC volunteering programs before applying but never took the step to take part. However, now I feel the time is right for me to go on such an adventure. From the very first moment I was looking in Ukraine because it was one of my life goals to visit and live in this country. I always thought that after my graduation I would go to Ukraine for a while. This kind of long-term experience you can do only at this age. Funny how the more you grow up the more time you have to lose to be a participant in such a project.

“But why Anna, why, Ukraine??”, was the question I heard on repeat from all my family and friends. Well, I always had a deep attraction for the eastern and slavic culture. This naturally led me to Russia, twice! While in Russia I really enjoyed the atmosphere of this eastern Slavic country. In Turin, my adopted city in Italy where I have been living for six years. I was lucky to have a lot of friends from the eastern countries like; Poland, Russia, and the Balkans just to name a few. I always have a lot of fun with these friends and enjoy learning more about their culture.

Being an expert in slavic cultures my per-knowledge of Ukraine sadly lacking. However, I did know some facts like; the catastrophe of Chernobyl (I’m sorry), Vladimir the first from Kyiv Rus’, the philosopher Skovoroda, some folk songs like Ochi chornye and Bublichki. I also knew that there are a lot more interesting sights to see beside Kyiv. For example, Odessa, L’viv and Ivan-Frankivsk.

These few things were already enough to intrigue my imagination and led me to this country. Ukraine has an immense heritage that must be discovered slowly. After reading the description of the programs. I liked the idea of organizing social cultural programs with direct contact with local people. I could really see myself enjoying this and believe it is the best way to experience a culture deeply. I felt I was ready for this challenge.

After finding out that I was selected by Pangeya Ultima. I just couldn’t wait until departure day. Unfortunately before my departure the pandemic situation in Italy got worse. I started to get very afraid and my anxiety started to haunt me. The question of could I still fully enjoy this unique with all the possibility it had to offer. Or would I be stuck doing my ESC online and miss out on the intercultural experience I had signed up for. In this sense, I must thank my Ukrainian correspondents who supported me and helped me a lot to overcome these fears.

Anyway, upon arriving in Ukraine, I understood it would not be easy being a one-hundred-percent Mediterranean person who loves the sun and the sea. I will especial miss taking long walks and enjoying the hot climate. I still don’t know why I always choose to seek the opposite lifestyle. That’s just the way I am and it will be an unsolved paradox of my life.

But I’m slowly realizing that Ukraine has a covert warmth: the human one. Ukraine has the warmth of its hospitality, kindness and of its colorful traditions and customs. Since I have been here, sometimes I forget I’m not in Italy anymore because of the extent people want to involve us in their culture and their everyday life. This is simply amazing and is what I was looking for when I applied for ESC. In just two weeks here, I’ve received for my birthday one of the most beautiful presents I could have desired. A magic red-tone Ukrainian vyshivanka (the typical Ukrainian woman dress)! It was a very special birthday that I will never forget.

Now my Italian friends will have to call me VyshivAn’ka (‘An’ka’ in Russian/Ukrainian is the abbreviation for the name of Anna) … maybe, the purpose of my permanence here was already intertwined in my name, like the flowerful squiggles of a vyshivanka. Who knows?)) Meanwhile, here I am, enjoying my Ukraine!
#pangeyaESC #youthinsight #interculturalyouthstudio

title: ESC “Global Difference Makers” in Bremen, Germany

data.text: Opportunity: European Solidarity Corps "Global Difference Makers"
Location: Bremen, Germany
Hosting Organization: Kulturzentrum Schlachthof e.V.

Information about organization: Kulturzentrum Schlachthof e.V. is a very big cultural organisation in Bremen (North-West Germany). The centre provides a space for young artists, musicians and actors to develop their skills and grow, for example through providing courses and workshops for children and young people in a variety of arts, or giving their professional stage to upcoming artists. The centre also frequently hosts top-class musicians, authors and artists, who attract big audiences. On a bi-monthly level, Kulturzentrum Schlachthof also publishes the cultural magazine “Z”, produced in their newspaper team. Located in the former slaughterhouse of Bremen, a huge building with industrial design, the organisation also provides professional training in stage and event tech. In the garden, the organisation frequently hosts outdoor concerts and events, and the neighbouring skating park is a popular place among the young people of the city. As a volunteer, you would become a part of their big, self-governed team that is divided into smaller subteams, for example the team that works with children in a theatre group, the media team that provides courses for young people in videography, and the music team that organises bandcamps of upcoming amateur musicians of Bremen. The cultural centre also organises a wide range of events – from climate change festivals to concerts, lectures and exhibitions, where your support would be needed particularly for the visibility – taking pictures, videos and managing the Instagram Channel of the organisation. You would be the first European Solidarity Corps volunteer hosted by Schlachthof. However, the organisation has frequently hosted interns and volunteers on other national and international programmes, and has a number of young trainees on their team.
Your tasks as a volunteer would include:
Helping out with the theatre workshops for very young children and youngsters
Helping with the organisation of bandcamps for older children from different parts of town
Supporting the media team with their workshops and production of videos in the media club
Taking part in the editorial team of the magazine issued by the cultural centre (depending on your German language skills and interest of course)
Take part in the backstage work of events (helping at the ticket and information desk, the logistics behind the scenes, the promotional materials etc.).
Taking pictures and videos during events and organising the Instagram and other social media visibility
Coming up with your own ideas for small events, workshops, exhibitions, …

Every Monday, you will meet with your primary supervisor to make a plan for the week, regarding which activities are going on in the house, where do you want to join, and what are your longterm plans in terms of own ideas and learning goals.
Don’t worry – you do not need to have prior experience in any of the areas or tasks described above. It is more important that you are motivated and curious to learn.
Accommodation, Logistics, Finances
You will be accommodated in a flat in Bremen with max. 4 other ESC volunteers. You will have your private room.

Bremen is a city in North-West Germany (around 500.000 inhabitants), not far from Hamburg and the North Sea coast. Bremen is a vibrant, multi-cultural city with a lot of young people and both a historical centre and newer areas of towns.
As an ESC volunteer, you will receive health insurance, monthly pocket money for food and other expenses (246€ + 150€). Travel costs will be reimbursed depending on the travel distance.

You will be supported by a Coordinator and a Mentor to help you get settled in your work place and the city of Bremen. You will also receive German language lessons of 1 hour per week (either Beginner level or Advanced Level).
As an ESC volunteer, you will also take part in the On-Arrival and Midterm Trainings, organised for all volunteers in Germany (free of charge for you).
You can apply, if you…
… are a resident of Ukraine
… between 18-30 years old (on the day you start your ESC)
… can communicate in English and/or German OR are very motivated to learn German throughout your ESC

… are interested in becoming a part of the cultural centre team, working with children and young people, curious to try yourself in photography and social media mangagement and contributing with your own ideas
… love to be creative and are passionate about making a positive change in society
… are an open-minded person, motivated to work in a team and with people from different religious, cultural and social backgrounds
European Solidarity Corps covers: accommodation, pocket money, money for food, transportation, insurance, visa assistance, training during the project and learning the national language.

The European Solidarity Corps is the new European Union initiative which creates opportunities for young people to volunteer or work in projects in their own country or abroad that benefit communities and people around Europe.
The young people who participate in the European Solidarity Corps will all agree with and uphold its Mission and Principles.

You can register for the European Solidarity Corps when you are 17 years old, but you cannot start a project until you are over 18. European Solidarity Corps projects will be available to people up to the age of 30 years old.

*Development center Pangeya Ultima is fully committed to protecting all applicants’ privacy. Information collected will be only used for the purpose of processing the applications, communicating with selected participants, for logistics purposes and travel costs reimbursement. Where sensitive, all the personal details of the applicants will be anonymised upon request. DC Pangeya Ultima pledges not to pass on the collected information to any other party besides those who are directly involved in the organization of the above project/event. By submitting their applications and providing access to personal information all applicants understand that they automatically give consent to processing and storing of own personal data.

Vinnytsia Photography club invites you to take part in a new and exciting opportunity we are hosting. Together with our parents' kvadart youth centre and Pangeya Ultima development centre we are hosting a photography Exhibition and looking for participants to enter their work. The theme is Lighting up Vinnytsia by night. Those who sign up will be asked to send in submissions of:
We ask for a total of four photos all with a caption
One photo taken at Night or at Dusk

One Photo that you feel best explains the city of Vinnytsia to a friend or foreigner.
and one Photo of your choice that you feel binds the other three photos together.

Email youthinsightproject@gmail.com

title: ESC “VOLUNTEERS FOR COMMUNITY SUPPORT” II Stage in Arad, Romania

data.text: Opportunity: European Solidarity Corps "VOLUNTEERS FOR COMMUNITY SUPPORT"
Location: Arad, Romania
Hosting Organization: Ofensiva Tinerilor
About organization:

The mission of Ofensiva Tinerilor is to provide young people with accessible educational opportunities, to help them reach their full potential. In this regard, educating young people in Arad to accept diversity and create a pleasant and safe environment for them is one of the main targets.

In addition, as active members of the European Peer Training Organization, Ofensiva Tinerilor is seeking to help fulfilling the common mission, to help young people embrace the diversity historically built up in this ancient city, but also to promote peer education as a way of social transformation.
Activities:
- Anti-discrimination workshops in schools, with more than 2000 beneficiaries;
- Training activities for teachers in the field of inclusion and non-formal education, with over 20 schools involved;
- Training activities for youth workers and young volunteers, with more than 200 persons trained who multiplied the programme with more than 2500 young people;
- Volunteering activities in favor of vulnerable groups, with more than 100 young people involved.
The intervention model includes a three-way approach:

1. Education – educating the youngsters to be more tolerant through specific training programmes. This will be achieved by organising weekly anti-discrimination and anti-bullying workshops in different secondary schools form Arad county, and other non-formal activities in partner schools with the aim of promoting European youth programs, the active participation of pupils in them and the stimulation of their own volunteering initiatives with vulnerable groups.

2. Inspiration – having the volunteers become role models for the young people they will be working with. This will be achieved through educational theatre activities in kindergartens and schools, with the volunteers using educational drama to promotes values such as empathy, friendship, respect for diversity and solidarity among children.

3. Action – involving the volunteers and local youngsters in activities that are in favour of vulnerable groups. This will be achieved through involving the volunteers and local youngsters in activities with our partners working with vulnerable groups (Vis de Copil association, CURUCUBEU day centre and other similar institutions from Arad), organising a “Boardgames Tour” (weekly game sessions with young people from privileged and disadvantaged neighbourhoods of the host community) and supporting the volunteers in developing own initiatives aimed at supporting persons and especially children from different socially challenging backgrounds are cared for.

Arad is situated on the West part of Romania, 50 km far from Hungarian border, being the 13th biggest city of Romania, with around 200.000 citizens. In the past Arad was called “little Vienna” because the architecture from the center of the 2 cities were quite similar. The river that runs through the city is called Mureș.
Important Aspects:
Accommodation – rented apartments, 2 persons/room, with access to bathroom (common), kitchen (common) and other utilities.
Meal – you will receive a monthly food allowance so you can arrange your own meals.
Local Transportation – you will receive a monthly tram ticket valid on all tram lines.
Internet – you will have access to internet at the accommodation and work place.
Washing machine and refrigerator – will be found in each apartment.
Profile of the volunteer:
- Between 18-30 years old;
- Resident of the sending country;
- Open and interested in working with persons from the vulnerable groups that we are targeting;
- Able to place this experience in a long-term perspective of personal development;
- Willing to learn new working methods and develop the necessary skills for organising the inclusive activities that will be necessary;
- Ready to adapt to a flexible working programme, but also to follow the responsibilities he/she will be assigned with;
- Being open to leave their comfort zone and integrate in a foreign country;
- Having difficulties in choosing a career or without employment options due to lack of practical experience.

title: The Challenges of ESC Volunteering During a Pandemic

data.text: Learning to Work Around Covid
Our New Team of ESC Volunteers
Introduction

With the arrival of COVID and its impact on our world. It's hard to imagine life in this Nieuw Normaal or new normal, a phrase constantly repeated in my home country of the Netherlands. Before coming to Ukraine for my ESC I thought carefully about how my projects would be effected by Covid. Would it be as valuable experience if all I did was sit be hide a computer zooming people all day. Thankfully this has not the happend and I am able to partake in a blend of online offline projects. However, that being said this ESC has not come without its ups and downs.
Dutch Cultural Class before lockdown
My Work

My work as an ESC volunteer at Pangeya Ultima Development Centre involves in a wide range of task. The four main directions which I focus on include running cultural and Language clubs for both Dutch and English. This is where I get to present my culture to the students and give them language lessons. The organising of a photography club. This includes running actives for the members like the up in coming photo exhibition which is being planned for mid February all going well. The setting up of an English debate club for people interested in debating politics and social topics relevant for today's youth. The hope is to teach and allow youth to discuss controversial topics in a health and constructive way. Lastly, I also work on writing my own articles about intercultural topics within the city of Vinnytsia and lead a group of creative writers to practices our story telling skills.
My Challenges

The greatest challenge faced was not surprisingly COVID restriction. This meant more administrative work, getting people to sign up of forehand to events and hopping those who had sign up would come to event and not waste the place someone else would have gladly take. The second was overcoming the challenges of having online events. For me this meant getting participants to use the online platforms used for conducting online lessons or events. To me this was the most challenging because there were times that the online tools simply didn't work or our internet content was poor. Furthermore, peoples technical skills or willingness to try new tools was an even bigger factor in the success of online event. This made using online tools difficult and sadly had an effect on the quality of work we tried to deliver.
Photo Club Members out on Excursion
What I have learned

Despite the challenges, the ESC experience has taught me a lot. Having to use online tools helped me see all new and cool ways of ingratiating online tools into your offline work. If used right online tools bring a new an exciting dimension to our work perversely not seen. The second is that with the constance changing in restrictions. Learning to be flexible is a must and not being so harsh on your own performance when things do not work out. I feel that this is the most important thing to remember. In life not all things can be foreseen and that sometimes things simply don't work out and that it is ok for this to happen.
Next Steps

Despite our challenges in 2020. I feel that our team will deliver some amazing results in 2021. During this lockdown period our photographies were able to work on their exhibition projects as we go into an empty city to take our photos. Our writers can keep writing through our online work book which helps our group continue to write even if we don't see each other physically. For the lockdown period our team in the debating projected have decided to make an online course for our debating club as a way to teach people all over the world. The goal is to carry on our work even if we can not meet physically.
Creative Writing Club
Conclusion

Though life has be tough in some places this year and learning to work in a pandemic environment has taught me many things. I am glad that I still choses to do my ESC and learnt how unpredictability can force you to explore new areas you may not have considered. For example, the making of an online course. This gives me hope that as we head into the spring the lessons learnt about working with COVID will only make our achievements that more spectacularly than in a per COVID world.

By the time we got acquainted with the Vinnytsia environment (about three or four weeks after our arrival), we were already planning our first trip within the Ukrainian borders. Although different destinations aroused our curiosity, after consulting some locals, we decided to go to Lviv for New Year’s Eve. The reason is simple and logical: pubs and cafes! Everyone we asked about Lviv ensured that it was simply amazing, especially in winter when you can stop by some cafeteria to restore from the winter cold and have a warm beverage.

When we got to the Vinnytsia station, it was like being there for the first time. Our arrival from Italy had been somehow rocambolesque and the late-night darkness did not let me observe the train station. This time, we chose a comfortable intercity train taking us to Lviv in less than 4 hours. Unluckily, a thick rain welcomed us in Lviv, so we got completely wet and frustrated while looking for the hostel. By 9pm, I was sitting in Virmenka café in the city center, with my coat completely wet and my hands holding tight the precious cup of Turkish coffee boiled in hot sand (strange time for an Italian to drink coffee, but the wetness of the situation really imposed it).

Luckily, three days of chilly and inspiring walks followed that stressful arrival night. We managed to see most of Lviv’s main attractions thanks also to Mykola, a tireless local who took us all around the Jewish quarter and surroundings of the city center. We also had a really good food experience, giving a try to both refined and street food places, and tasting lots of cakes and coffees. Coffee was definitely a nice surprise: I generally struggle to get satisfactory coffee when I am abroad (we Italians are complicated people). This was not the case anyhow; the coffee was enjoyable and in line with Italian standards. Most of the cafeteria also had fashionable furniture which was clearly inspired by the belle epoque and Austrian period of the 19th and early 20th century. The coffee experience in Lviv is just something amazing!

Among all the attractions we have been visiting during our stay, there was one detail which particularly stroke my attention, something you can notice only if you look around carefully or hang around with some expert local. I am talking about a little statue of a lion, not a Lviv’s lion, but a Venetian one! I noticed it in a completely random situation when we were queuing to enter the famous pub Kryvka. By chance, I raised my glance on top of the arch noticed that there was a Venetian lion on it. I told my travel mates to look at it, but they were mostly skeptical about my observation, saying that it was just Lviv’s heraldic lion. I observed it better, and I pointed out that the lion was holding a book in its paws with the Latin inscription “Pax tibi Marce evangelista meus” (something like “peace be unto thee O Mark my evangelist”). Saint Mark is indeed the patron saint of the city of Venice, that evidence was already enough strong to prove that I was right. Mykola agreed with me and stated that it was a Venetian lion for real. That palace was built in the 16th century by Venetian merchants, whose commercial power and interests stretched until the florid city of Lviv. By checking on the internet, I found that the owner of the palace was Antonio Massari, an ambassador of the Venetian Republic who was trading precious fabrics in the city of Lviv.

The trip ended with other four relaxing hours of Intercity train until Vinnytsia. I believe that you cannot really feel at home in a place until you do not start a trip from there. This was my first travel around Ukraine starting from Vinnytsia, and finally, while looking through the taxi window along Soborna street, I really felt at home.

The historic L’viv city center is worldwide known as one of the most beautiful in Europe. Actually, in 1998 it was listed by UNESCO as a part of “World Heritage”. If you see it for the first time, you easily get the reason. His little old city is an agglomerated of different architecture styles. Here Austrian-Hungary, Poland, Italian renaissance intersect each other, giving you the sensation of living in another time.

Among the hundred churches that characterize the city center of L’viv, there is one which is hidden and set between cafés and restaurants, the Armenian church. Located in Virmenka Street (not casually, since Virmenka means Armenian in Ukrainian language), this little church is one of the monuments that impressed me the most. I did not expect to find an Armenian church in L’viv, in the middle of Europe. I was so curious that I asked the Father about the history of the church. He explained to me that one of the most populous Armenian communities was here, in Galicia region. After the end of Armenian Cilician Kingdom, due to the Arabic and Turkish invasions in XI century, a wave of Armenian migration moved to Russia and Europe, where colonies of Armenian merchants started up. After Theodosia and Crimea, the favorite destination of Armenian migrants was the city of L’viv. The Mother of God’s Assumption Cathedral Church is the only one of the original five Armenian churches that survived and that is still acting. It was built a first time in 1363, but a fire burned its wooden foundations, and the church was rebuilt in XVI century.

Looking at it is like jumping throw space and time. For a few second, you easily forget of being in Ukraine and suddenly, you find yourself in the heart of Caucasus. The bell tower and the cloister remind me about the beautiful monastery complex of Sevan. I asked the father if there was some connection with it, but he explained to me that the church was inspired by the ancient Armenian Cathedral in the city of Ani (modern Turkey, on the border with Armenia). Ani is now a half ghost city in the desert, but less than one thousand years ago it was the Capital of Armenian Kingdom, known as City of 1001 churches. Probably, Armenians wanted to recreate this church here, in a “securer” place, because they wanted to remember the glory of their culture and their past, a past now almost forgotten. Quite coincidentally, both the two churches, the one in L’viv and the one in Ani, belong to the UNESCO Worldwide Heritage.

In contrast with this external ancient style, the interiors are decorated by the exquisite shades of art nouveau frescos which literally impressed me. Why modernist décors in an Armenian church? At a first glance, I thought it was the work of German painter Franz von Stuck, with his visionary and mysterious style. Almost close. The artist is a polish painter, Jan Henryk de Rosen who decorated the church under the commission of the local Archbishop. Among the frescos, tender illuminated by the warm lights of candles, two of them caught my attention, The Beheading of John the Baptizer and the Funeral of Saint Odilon. In the latter, specifically, three people handle the lifeless body of the saint. They are the personification of the time: the past with the uncovered face, the present with open eyes and the future with an open face but with close eyes. The iconography of death and life is something which is always interesting. It makes you think a lot…

After the church, we went through a little street around it. With my camera in the hand, I saw through my lens a mural of a face familiar to me. He was the director Sergey Paradzhanov, probably one of the most famous Armenian directors who lived in Ukraine. His works contributed to transmit another image of his homeland, a country rich of beauty, intertwining it with the multiculturality of Ukrainian traditions. A charming portrait of a less known Ukraine is offered in Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors, a movie about Hutsuli community of the Carpathians. Next to his portrait, I read the writing: Knigi zabutych predkiv (Books of Forgotten Ancestors). Indeed, it's him.

After a second wave of migration due to the genocide in the XX century, and the third one after the USSR's disintegration, the Armenian community of Ukraine became one of the largest in the world (about 100 thousand people). Today in whole country there are 14 Armenian churches that unite the Armenian people in a unique big family, under the blue-yellow flag of Ukraine.

One month ago, in Vinnytsya, the Italian Language Club has started. Every Tuesday the Italian volunteers for Pangeya Ultima, Anna and Matteo, teach the language through a non-formal approach. The lessons have not just the intention to teach the language like in boring school time but to do it through a deep immersion in the Italian culture. Music, food, Italian nature, traditions are the main topic.

We all know that Visual Art and Media are also a big part of the culture. That's how the idea of an Italian Cinema Club arose. Italijs'kino wants to be an additional club of the Italian language one, where also cinephiles can be involved. Still, one of the goals is to show another part of Italian cinema history that is less known abroad. Italian cinema is not only Celentano's movies or easy modern comedies, but it has a huge tradition that did not penetrate the borders.

The last Thursday, in #Cherdak space, we had an example. The first event of the Cinema Club has begun with a masterpiece, one of the 100 Italian movies to be saved: Antonio Pietrangeli's work Io la conoscevo bene (I knew her well). Although the film is from the '60s, it is not dated at all, on the contrary, it gets to know with Italian society of economic boom. Antonio Pietrangeli tells us the story of Adriana, a beautiful and naive girl from the Italian province who moved to Rome to become an actress. Night parties, dances, and spending time on the beach compose her existence. Every hairstyle brings new encounters with a new man she falls in love with, and from whom she receives only humiliations. She keeps living alone in the private world of her apartment, between vinyl and beauty care. But beyond this superficial ingenuousness, Adriana hides a load which will lead her to do something unexpected to those who know her, spectator included.

The importance of this movie is due not only to the director but also to the cast and the soundtrack that frames the plot. In the movie we find some of the most famous Italian actors like Stefania Sandrelli, Nino Mandrefi, and Ugo Tognazzi; the music is composed by Piero Piccioni who along with Ennio Morricone and Nino Rota wrote the most beautiful Italian soundtracks. Besides the compositions, in the movie, we can listen to Italian songs, like the ones of Mina, Ornella Vanoni, and Sergio Endrigo.
Aframe of the movie Io la conoscevo bene

This proves that Italian culture is much more than Cutugno, Celentano, and Albano. Or it would be better to say that it is not only that.
This was the first Italian cinema meeting but in the following events you will know other news, songs, actors and curious facts. Stay tuned, cinephiles and Italian enthusiasts!

title: Відгук Вікторії з проекту у Литві

data.text: В Литві на проекті я вже два місяці.

Що можу сказати, я дуже задоволена та вдячна, що я тут. Я живу в маленькому містечку в комфортних умовах. В садочку дуже дружелюбна та легка атмосфера, всі з повагою до мене відносяться, допомогають з реалізацією ідей.

Кожний тиждень я в новій групі де я проводжу різні активності, ігри та створюю навчальні матеріали для дітей. Спочатку було складно через мовний бар’єр, але десь через місяць я вже розуміла дітей та зараз досить вільно спілкуюсь з ними. Звісно є і невеликі мінуси, але вони не залежать від організації чи садочка.

Литва вже майже місяць закрита і не дозволено навіть в інше місто виїхати. В самому місті теж все закрито окрім супермаркетів, тому нажаль окрім прогулянки в парку розніманітнити своє дозвілля неможливо.

title: Фотовиставка  "CAPTURING THE SOUL OF VINNYTSIA BY NIGHT"

data.text: Завдяки такому колу спілкування на тему створення фото та фіксуванню моменту нам вдалось об’єднати таке ком’юніті крутих людей, які прагнуть розвиватись більше у цій сфері.

У середу, 3 березня, відбулась презентація фото-виставки учасників клубу під назвою"CAPTURING THE SOUL OF VINNYTSIA BY NIGHT". Вони працювали протягом декількох місяців разом вивчали теорію, практикували свої навички та ось показали результат.

Презентували даний проект голова нашої організації Ярослав Геращенко та наші партнери Вінницький обласний молодіжний центр "Квадрат", де і проходить виставка. На відкритті були присутні як самі фотографи, так і гості виставки🧐 Відвідувачі побачили ці надзвичайно дивовижні фотографії та уже віддали свої голоси за ті світлини, які найбільше сподобались📸

Нагадуємо, що виставка триватиме з 3 березня по 14 березня, а голосування - до 11 березня📆 Тому не гай часу та проголосуй за найкраще фото просто зараз за цим посиланням: docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScl3Ak7xc6rnKGSok3U-WoGl2K5UonbDOEsHf_JB0nhskhXYA/viewform?usp=send_form&hl=en.

А після голосування за фото, вибери ще автора, який сподобався тобі найбільше своїм антуражем, креативом, підходом та іншим)

In Vinnytsia, there is an active photo club for amateurs and professionals called "Vinnytsia Photography". Now the club is operated under the leadership of a foreign volunteer Paul Morgenstern. It is a community of like-minded people who share knowledge and experience between one another in the art of photography.
Thanks to this circle of communication on the subject of creating a photo and capturing the moment, we were able to unite such a community of cool people who want to develop more in this field.

On Wednesday, the third of March, a presentation of the club members’ photo exhibition entitled "CAPTURING THE SOUL OF VINNYTSIA BY NIGHT" took place. They worked together for several months studying theory and practicing their skills, and eventually showed the results.

This project was presented by the head of our organization Iaroslav Gerashchenko and our partners Vinnytsia Regional Youth Center "Kvadrat", where the exhibition actually takes place. Both photographers and guests of the exhibition were present at the opening. Visitors saw these extremely amazing photos and have already given their votes for the photos they liked the most.

And after voting for the photo, choose another author who you liked the most for his entourage, creativity, approach, etc.).

title: How the wrong Chernivtsi lead us to Berdychiv

data.text: Two months after our arrival in Ukraine, we decided to discover less touristic cities in the country. Our first choice was to go to Chernivtsi but after discovering that we had booked tickets to the wrong Chernivtsi, for there are another Chernivtsi in Vinnytsyan reagion. We then decided why not go to Berdychiv instead?

Berdychiv is a city commonly known for being one of Ukrainians historic Jewishs capitals. Before the Second World War, the Jewish people made up 80% of the population until the Nazis decomated the Jewish population and all traces of their existence. Outside the city’s limits it’s still to find the mass graves of where the Naizs carried out their acts against the Jewish people. Today the Jewishs community is made up of not more than a few hundred inhabitants. What remains of their culture are the three Synagogues (actually, one of them is out) and a Jewish cemetery. This one in particular impressed us a lot. We’ve never seen such a large Jewish cemetery before so we didn't know what to expect. The scenario was unbelievable. A lawn of grey graves occupied a big part of the field. It was like these graves were growing directly from the ground. A special space was dedicated to Rabbin’s grave Levy Yitzchak, as far as we know an important personality in the Jewish world.

Berdychiv is not only famous for the Jewish culture. Actually, we went there to visit the museum of the writer Joseph Conrad. Why a museum of an English writer in Ukraine? Well, Conrad was actually a Polish who emigrated to England when he was around 18 (his original name was Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski). In 2015 the Polish Minister of Culture dedicated a little museum in his native city. The museum is pretty small, but it lets you go back over the main events of the life of the writer.

Our visit to the museum was led by Camilla, a kind Nun of Carmelite sisters. We met her thanks to Eduard, a cheerful man from Odessa, who worked in the shop of the Church. When we first told him we were from the Netherlands and Italy, he couldn’t believe his eyes. Italians, here? I traveled to all Italian ports: Naples, Venice, Genua, Sicily.. Sicily! There I have my best friend, Federico! I will never forget him.” He told us something more about the main Church of the city, where we met him and where the Monastery of the Nun had placed. “Here every year a lot of people come to visit the icon of the Virgin Mary, you can see it upon the altar! There are only six of them in the world! Wait, I’ll give you this”. He gave us a little picture of the icon with the Polish version of Lord’s Prayer. Then we kept talking about his life. He has been living in Berdychiv for years to help his mother, but he really misses the sea and Odessa.

His spontaneous way of approaching people electrified our trip as he gave us tips about what to see in the city and how to go back to Vinnytsia. “Don’t miss to visit Saint Barbara Church, where the French writer got married, Balzac! Balzac! Did you know?”. We did, actually, but we did not know that his wife was a noble Polish, Madame Hanska. Actually, after seeing the Church we were a little bit disappointed. Insided it was almost empty and the exterior walls were pink. For us it was pretty unusual and strange…

Balzac and Conrad are not the only names related to this city. Berdychiv is also the native place of Vassily Grossmann, it is still possible to find the house where he was born. It is strange how an almost unknown city in Ukraine had so many stories to share. This taught us that no matter where you go, every place you visit always has history beyond it.

We kept walking through the streets of the city, passing through the main park dedicated to Taras Shchevchenko. In Ukraine every city has a park dedicated to Schevchenko, even the smallest one. Unfortunately, the grey cloudy sky damped our mood as the temperature dropped below -10, only to be made worse by the wind in the half empty city. Only in a little square, with a children playground, we met a group of little kids playing with each other. They were startled by us, probably because of our cameras, or just the way we were dressed. We guess they were wondering “why three touristed decided to come here in February?”

The answer is simply. Ukraine is not only Kyiv and L’viv but so much more. It has a rich and complex history with many stories scattered across the land which once found fit together like a jigsaw puzzle with unique stories that show the real Ukraine. This is the Ukraine we want to explore and get to know!
Anna, Paul and Matteo
Photo by Anna Mangiullo and Paul Morgenstern

Моя однорічна пригода з Європейським Корпусом Солідарності у Болгарії добігла до свого завершення. Рік минув дуже швидко, але в той же час це був надзвичайно довгий та насичений рік. Насичений він був різними подіями тож тепер, озираючись назад, я хочу зібрати все, що сталося зі мною цього року докупи, всі мої злети і падіння, весь досвід і, звичайно, всіх людей, яких я зустріла протягом цього року і які кардинально змінили моє життя.
Отже, рік тому назад, 2 березня 2020 року, літак з Києва зі мною на борту прибув до аеропорту Софії і моя пригода з Фундацією «Смокіня» розпочалася!

Мене тепло зустріли у Пловдиві, в квартирі для волонтерів яблуку ніде було впасти! Я зустрілася з волонтерами з минулого проекту, які власне відїжджали додому: Агіта, Алекса та Крістіна з Латвії та Мелані і Мей Лінг з Німеччини. Нас було шість людей, повсюди було дуже гамірно, життя і події так і вирували навколо, все було настільки різноманітним тож я із задоволенням пірнула у цей вир подій разом з усіма.

А потім прийшло «ВОНО», то нещастя, що розділило весь світ на «до» і «після». Попередні волонтери почали дуже швидко виїжджати з Болгарії, і вже через 2 тижні я залишилася сама. Перший тиждень був найскладнішим, я навіть спала із увімкненим світлом пару ночей. Цілий світ заглибився у невизначеність, і всі відчували тривогу.

Тоді я отримала велику підтримку від своїх друзів та команди. Навіть в Інтернеті ми продовжували робити щоденні зустрічі, виконувати деякі завдання для організації, і це приносило надію, що скоро настануть кращі часи. Крім того, тоді я почала робити онлайн-курси мови, що додало мені сильної впевненості в собі і відволікало від сумних думок.

Коли нарешті прийшло літо, то життя знову завирувало. Відчувалося, що все позаду, і всі почали прокидатися після довгого зимового сну. «Смокіня» отримала нову домівку, яку треба було привести до ладу. І,звичайно, кликали пригоди, тож я почала відкривати для себе Болгарію.

Вересень завжди був для мене особливим часом. Бо навіть зараз, після стільки років після випускного, я пов’язую це з новим навчальним роком, новим початком, а також у мене у вересні День народження. 4 вересня Фундація &quot;Смокіня&quot; офіційно відкрила свої двері для молоді у Пловдиві, і осінь була дуже насиченою на події, з різними злетами, падіннями та завданнями. Одним з моїх найбільших досягнень я вважаю організацію розмовного клубу російської мови, який став проходи регулярно що два тижні і навіть зараз, коли я вже поїхала, члени клубу продовжують збиратися і проводити час разом. Також сім'я «Смокіні» стала більшою - на борт прибули Роза, Крістін, Калда, Лоїс та Владан!

Я вважаю, що мій досвід дуже унікальний через усілякі карантини, локдауни, запобіжні мірі та таке інше. Але навіть під час мого пандемічного року в Болгарії я дізналася та навчилася багато нового. Наприклад, я навчилася як писати волонтерські проекти, вивчила болгарську мову, і останнє, але не менш важливе: як святкувати свій успіх, замість того, щоб його ігнорувати! Я зустріла багато людей, які стали для мене особливими і розкрила саму себе з нової, до цього часу невідомої мені самій, сторони.
Зараз я повертаюся з Болгарії з набагато ширшим поглядом на те, що і як робити у своєму житті, і я не кажу Болгарії «Прощавай…», я кажу «До скорої зустрічі неодмінно ще не раз!»
Дякую за цей рік!

18 - 30 years old;
is available for volunteering for a period of 6,5 months: from May to November 2021;

data.text: Opportunity: Weltwärts
Dates: September 2022 – September 2023 (12 month)
Location: Halle, Germany
Coordinating Organization: Friedenskreis Halle e.V.
About organization

The association works in three areas:
1. peace politics: actions, campaigns, exhibitions, presentations, lectures and workshops next to local and regional networking
2. Peace education: own workshops, seminars and trainings in Halle, the region and abroad in cooperation with local to international partners next to mediation of offers and trainers
3. Peace services – international voluntary service: consultation and information for interested persons and organisations next to hosting, sending and coordinating within „weltwärts“ and „European voluntary service“

"We have a dynamic understanding of peace: We do not understand peace as a state of affairs, not as a far-off goal and not as just as the absence of war. To us peace is a path towards a cooperative, fair and non-violent living together in diversity by which self-fulfilment and freedom of each individual become possible".
"Basic themes and guiding values of our work are: active non-violence, constructive as well as civil conflict management, living democracy, transcultural diversity and global justice".
Field of engagement and activities of the volunteer

The voluntary service mainly is office work and educational work with children, youth and adults.
The volunteer will mainly support the area “Peace education” inclusive attached projects.
The focus of the educational work, especially the work on political development and civil conflict management abroad, lies on schools and nurseries.
What to expect?
25 days of accompanying seminars, midterm and final trainings, anti-discrimation and political participation seminars. All expenses connected to the seminars and trainings are covered
German language training and support
Public German health insurance
A separate room in a shared apartment
Allowance - 350 Euro per month
30 working hours per week

Service related activities (around 8h/week): Active participation in accompanying programme, implementation of own project, occupation with and/or engagement in topics and activities of (local) civil society
Mentors with work and one peer mentor who's from the city
Monthly tram ticket or bicycle
Visa support and visa fee coverage
24 holidays off.
Volunteers profile - General

• weltwärts: 18-28yrs (exceptions can be made, when reasonable)
• School graduation or comparable personal suitability
• Knowledge of English and willingness to learn German starting in home country
• Openess to the approach of the service as learning and peace service
• Willingness to get involved in civil society after the service
• Specific profile (certain interest and/or abilities) for at least one of the places of assignment we cooperate with (s. profiles places of assignment).
Which places of assignment (POA) Friedenskreis Halle cooperates with?

• Kinder und Jugendhaus e.V. and Bürgerhaus AlternativE (open youth work with kids 10-18yrs)
• Clare Zetkin e.V. (childrens home for kids 6-18yrs)
• Friedenskreis Halle e.V. (educational and office work)
• Kita Bartholomäus , Kita Marktspatzen, KindElternZentrum Lieskau (nursery for kids 1-6yrs)
• Lebenstraum Halle e.V. (living group with disabled adults)
• Kulturwerkstatt Grüne Villa e.V. (social-cultural centre)
• Anlaufstelle S.C.H.I.R.M. (drop-in centre for young persons 18-30yrs)
• Passage 13
If you have any questons, please, write us to pangeya.ultima.mobility@gmail.com
N/B Candidates from Vinnytsia and Vinnytsia region will receive the preference. Applications will be processed on a rolling basis. As soon as proper candidates are found, the call will be closed
weltwärts covers: accommodation, pocket money, money for food, transportation, insurance, visa assistance, training during the project and learning the national language.

weltwärts is all about engagement in development issues, global learning and interacting as equals. It brings people together in and from Germany, Asia, Africa, Latin America, Oceania and Eastern Europe. The programme focuses on non-formal learning on a mutual basis and strengthening of international partnerships.

The programme, whose name translates as “worldwards”, was launched in 2008 by the Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) to support young people looking to take action for the good of our One World. Since then, going “worldwards” has been possible through the programme’s development volunteer service and, since 2016, through “weltwärts – Extracurricular exchange projects in the context of Agenda 2030”.

Each sub-programme has a comprehensive quality system and receives 75% of its funding from the BMZ. The remaining share comes from the civil-society organisations that implement the service. The administrative and financial coordination of the programme is carried out by Engagement Global’s weltwärts Coordination Unit.
The weltwärts volunteer service is a joint operation run by the BMZ, civil-society organisations and past volunteers, with decisions regarding the steering of the programme taken jointly.

title: Behind the Scenes of Capturing the Soul of Vinnytsia by Night Club Photo Exhibition of 2021

data.text: The Making of Vinnystsia Photography's Club first Exhibition of 2021
Our Method and Mission

Our main goal is non formal education with our slogan "learning by doing" In order to active this goal we use small projects for members to work towards which incorporate skills taught in our workshops which help guide participants through the various task we set out for them. Through the completion of these task and than the final product to visualise their work. We hope to not only teach members skils but to inspire armature photographers in creating good photos.
Training our Technical know how
Technique Training Workshop

In the first few weeks of our project we spent our meetings looking at basic photography concepts like using light. Specificity how to add light to photos eg. candle light or neon night. Next we looked at night photography and the techniques need to produce good photos at night. With the completion of these sessions it was time to start the practical part and release the enter criteria for submissions to our exhibition. The criteria for participants were, send four photos. One, had to be a photo taken at night. The second, a photo taken with neon lights. These two were to test the technical ability of participants. The third, a photo of the city Vinnytsia and the fourth, A creative selfie. the last two are to let the photographers use their creativity when taking photos.
Night photography and Excursions
Night Photography

we spent two sessions going out into the night taking photos for our submissions. Once we had collected a large sample of pictures. We choses the best ones to bring to our photo labs. Here we could share our photos we had taken and receive feedback how to improve them in both post production and what to look out for next time we take photos. The model was repeated once again with a day time excursion inn the city to help students find photos for the category Vinnytsia to me. This was once again followed by a photo lab to discuss how to improve the photos before we hand in our final submission.
Exhibition day

Our exhibition began on the 3rd of March and ran to the 12th. During this time, people who visited could vote on which photo they liked the best. On the final day these votes were counted and the winners received a small symbolic prize to congratulate them on their hard work. This was than followed by celebratory drinks in a restaurant and thus, concluded our first exhibition. During our next adventure we will be looking at the topic of digital story telling. If this sound interesting to you and you wish to partake our program or you simply just want to come take photos with us. data.text: Title of the project: ESC TEAM: Time for Engagement, Action and Mentorship
Places: 3 participants
Location: Blagoevgrad, Bulgaria
Hosting Organization: Active Bulgarian Society

Information about the project: The TEAM project's main goal is to create a learning environment for young people with fewer opportunities from partner and program countries. We want the participants to enhance their social capital and get on their path of social development. At the same time, the project aims to contribute to the reinforcement of intercultural dialogue, promote solidarity, youth policy, active citizenship, and European awareness in the area of Blagoevgrad. We will provide young people with an opportunity to undertake volunteering mobility in a youth organization that is an active youth work provider in its area, as ABS is in Blagoevgrad. Thus, we will create a win-win situation: the local community of Blagoevgrad greatly benefits from raised intercultural awareness and European citizenship, understanding better the main principles and specific objectives of the ESC Program, while the volunteers acquire unique knowledge that impacts their employability potential and the practices they learn can be reduplicated in their home communities. Moreover, the skills and competencies the participants will acquire through participating in TEAM are transferable, which means that they will help them in the future to find a job or when applying for a university degree, internship, or other relevant fields.
PARTICIPANT'S PROFILE:
18 - 23 years old;
able to communicate in English;
motivated, proactive, and with an initiative to carry out their own projects;
ready to work in an intercultural atmosphere;
is able to adapt to new situations and enjoys teamwork;
has experience organizing workshops and activities, and is willing to learn.
How will you benefit from the project:
you will develop your soft skills and your technical skills;
you will be able to express yourself more comfortably in English;
you will gain creative and innovative ideas;
you will make friends from all over the world;
you will learn how to plan and organize events;
you will increase your level of active citizenship.
Food and Pocket money: Volunteers will get 80 euros per month (or the equivalent in Bulgarian currency) for food and 120 euros for pocket money.

Accommodation: Volunteers will be accommodated in a shared room with another volunteer (of the same sex) in their own fully furnished flat, with all needed kitchen utensils, which is situated 15 minutes walking to the office and the city center. The flat has all the necessary facilities for living.
P.S. Costs related to COVID19 tests are NOT covered by the project

Journeys always surprise me. People I will meet, sceneries I will see. They all come up when you haven't even thought that it could happen to you. While so, every adventure needs the courage to leave behind your comfort zone to discover other cultures. You gotta leave the home you lived since you know yourself. As for me, I was curious about the things happening somewhere out there. So, I made my decision and took that plane to be a volunteer in Ukraine.

After arriving in Ukraine and when I took an old soviet train to the Vinnitsyia I felt that I was in a completely different place. When the lady on the train helped us to make our bed on the sleeping train (we did not know how to do it) I was surprised by how people were able to help and care about each other even though we didn't speak the same language. I just thought the language was not common but feelings were uniting us. Feeling to care, feeling to help. I was feeling that I am in another episode of life that I experience the whole life again from a different perspective.

Finally, I arrived in Vinnytsia and the city welcomed us greatly with a sunny day. We took a walk with our supervisor Olia and visited Vishenka lake. Then Olia showed us how to cook Ukrainian pancakes. Pancakes are always delicious but I’m sure Olia has some secrets to make them the best. By the way, the good thing about the pancakes is that I can cook them myself now.

Now, I have been here for 3 weeks and I met lots of new friends from different countries. I start to belong to where I live and be a part of this life here. Everyday I think that it is the best day, and I'm astonished when the next day turns out even better. Such as today we went to a town called Voronovytsya and we watched the Ukrainian traditional performance and next week we plan to stay overnight in a Ukrainian village, so I’m very happy to have these adventures in my life. Once again I remind myself that the best things never come when you’re in your comfort zone and I am very happy to make my journey to Vinnytsia.

title: “You’ve got this!” Charlotte’s story of becoming a ESC volunteer

data.text: After finishing my bachelor's degree in history I found myself wondering what to do next in life. University was a tough, but mostly great phase in my life that I can happily look back on. After this studying phase, I started thinking about myself: What is my passion? What do I really want in life? What personal goals do I wish to achieve?

My whole life has taken place in Amsterdam, a vibrant, busy city that never bored me. But then, the need to discover new places and people started growing in me. The answer to my many questions arose to me. I had to go completely out of my comfort zone: being a volunteer. With this idea in my mind, I came across the website of the European Solidarity Corps. This program of the EU helps young people like me to take part in projects that benefit communities, either abroad or in their own country. These projects offer an empowering, unforgettable experience as well as the chance to bring change while developing your skills and competences. It all seemed too good to be true and I immediately came into contact with a Dutch sending organisation. Together we discussed the offered projects and which one suits me best. Soon, my eye fell on the projects of Pangeya Ultima in Vinnytsia.

In many Ukrainian publications, Vinnytsia is always ranked at the top of the list of best cities to live in Ukraine. After googling Vinnytsia, I could see why. This location has a unique charm combined with historical monuments, nature and architecture. Besides the city's coziness, the projects of organization Pangeya Ultima also attracted me: promoting intercultural dialogue, active citizenship and non-formal education. This empowerment of youth inspires me and I want to play a part in this as well. At the same time, I have the opportunity to develop my media skills, something I've always been interested in. Hence, this creative environment is just what I need!

Still, making a decision was hard. Before coming to Vinnytsia as a volunteer, I honestly had no pre-knowledge of slavic countries. Therefore, I was scared to immerse myself in this foreign culture and learn this language. Mostly because of my personal fears and insecurities. After long talks with family and friends I finally made the decision to take the plunge.

Now that I'm in Vinnytsia I learn and see new things every day. Of course, at the beginning it was a bit hard and very new for me. But these things are part of life and makes it much more adventurous and enjoyable. I've noticed that I'm starting to fall in love with Ukrainian culture and its friendly people who have fully embraced me and helped me to adapt. It’s all so heartwarming and exactly what I hoped for when I signed up to be an ESC volunteer.

Looking back at myself debating whether going abroad is the right choice for me: I’m so glad that I made this decision. For the first time, I really stepped out of my comfort zone. One year ago I couldn’t even have thought that I’d go abroad, but look at me now! For people like me, still debating whether going abroad is the right step for them, just don’t lose yourself in self-doubt and insecurities. Going abroad and being a volunteer is a great way to meet new people, learn about cultures and about yourself. You’ve got this!

title: Don’t think twice, it is my only advice! Fatih's arrival story

data.text: Hey guys! I am Fatih from Turkey. It is time to answer the question which is:

“Why did I choose this project in Vinnytsia and why am I in Ukraine now?” Let’s start from the beginning. After graduation from the university I was not sure what I was going to do next. Actually, I started to do my master’s degree but I was not satisfied with it. Since I have already had some abroad experience, I know that international environment brings new surprises and challanges to my life. So, I decided to look for some volunteering activities on ESC website and made up my mind to apply for several projects. The project in Vinnytsia distinguished from others because it was a mix of urban and rural life. That’s why I felt so excited to have an opportunity to take part in this project. So, I wrote my motivation letter and prepared my CV for the application. After getting positive feedback from Iaroslav, I started to learn more about the city and the country. To be honest, I found out about the existance of Ukraine when I was 6 or 7, thanks to Andriy Shevschenko, the striker of the legendary Italian team A.C. Milan. Although I did not have extensive knowledge about Ukraine, I knew it as a country which unites west and east in some way, has experienced severe difficulties but somehow managed to stand firmly. Over the years, I have learned more about Ukraine and in 2020 I visited Lviv and Kyiv. These cities represent two different regions and sides of this beautiful country. Actually, my first impression was very positive. Maybe that’s why I chose to come to Vinniytsia without doubts.

When it comes to my trip to Ukraine, it was totally smooth and fast. I am saying this because I and Ibrahim were warmly welcomed by Piotr in Lviv airport. We had a short city tour and then had dinner together. It was time to get on the train to Vinnytsia where I would live for nine months 😊 I will not talk a lot about train ride because Ibrahim described it very well. Instead, I want to thank to dear Babushka (ti kak maya mama!) who helped us a lot when we were struggling to make our beds. A few hours later it was time to meet a man who helped us a lot during this preparation period. Of course, I am talking about Iaroslav. He welcomed us with a Turkish cap on his head :D and made me smile and feel more relax. Then we went to our old Sovietic but at the same time cozy and cute apartment with pink wallpapers. When I finally got to bed after the long trip, I said to myself: “Now you are in Ukraine, buddy, no jokes anymore”. Next morning we met our best Ukrainian teacher Olya, we planned to prepare something sweet, mlyntsi (pancakes), and I think we did a good job for first time 😉 After having the first meeting with volunteers and mentors I realized that I made a right decision to come and live here for 9 months. To be honest, I watched some documentary serials like Winter on Fire and Chernobyl to know more about Ukraine but that was just tragical and sad parts of this beautiful country. After spending two weeks with locals I saw there is no bad behavior from them. They are friendly and warm people, who respect foreigners. I also want to mention about Vareniky (I knew it as pierogi in Poland) but tasting in Ukraine, I gotta say it is much better here (especially Sasha’s homemade ones).

I would also like to mention about our trip to Stina and Voronaviytsia because these places still have its own traditions and cultures. If you want to learn more about Ukraine you can visit any village or town here. Meeting with young and old generation at the same time, gives you perspective about changes and different lifes in Ukraine. Maybe a year or a few years later, new volunteers will read my blog about Pangeya Ultima and Vinnytsia. I assure you it is worth coming and experiencing new things here. Even if I have been living here for only for three weeks, it is obvious that these people in Pangeya really take care of us and give us opportunities to discover ourselves better. So don’t think twice it is my only advice 😉

title: True village experience in Stina, Ukraine

data.text: It’s almost exactly a month since I have arrived in Vinnytsia as a volunteer, but in Stina I have been only for a one-day trip so far. This time we are committed to live in the rural area for three days.

The four guys from three different countries set off. After having a “smooth-road drive” we arrived at our house. The first thing we did was cleaning and then we planned what to do next few days. Soon we had a chance to meet Uncle Nikola, who lives a few houses away. He and his cute granddaughter brought us some potato and drinks. We talked about different things even if I didn’t totally understand the language 😊 In the afternoon, we met youngsters and started our teaching English section, since one of my reasons of being there is teaching English to them. And they offered us to have a walk around the village. I was amazed when I saw the river and beautiful nature. We visited a stone building which had three floors and resembled a cave. It was fascinating and creepy at the same time. Next we were shown a school, a church and a graveyard from the 17th century and that was the end of our excursion. In the evening we made a fire, had a talk, and ate together. After a while we felt tired and went to sleep.

Next day after having breakfast, we decided to clean a yard of a house 100m away from ours. After working for a few hours, I realized that living in a village makes me feel more alive. Then we had a nice meeting with youngsters, playing games, singing songs, listening to our favourite musics and sharing funny stories. Then it was time to cook potato with eggs on the fire. It was a team work; some of us made a fire, others cut vegetables for salad. By the way, our meal was delicious 😉

The third day of the journey started with beautiful sunlight in our house. After going through some morning routine, I went out to the yard. My task for that day was to carry stones to the place where a new wall will be built. The mission was simple but needed a bit of man power. While we were working, Alejandro prepared lunch for us. After eating we decided to go and help Uncle Nikola with planting potato. I am an agricultural engineer but I have never had any practical experience before. He was happy to see us. He showed me what to do and I started to dig soil and place three small potato seeds into each hole. Every potato has about six or seven buds. It means each three potatoes give about twenty big potatoes. In an hour we came back to our house for a meeting with Iaroslav and went to Liana’s garden. She decided to live in Stina after being here for the festival two years ago. And now she and her husband are engaged in permaculture. We had a nice meeting with her. She told us about her plans, showed us around the house and gave some interesting details about permaculture (plants growing method). After saying goodbye to her, we returned the house because youngsters had a plan for us!! VARENIKI! It was time to work as a team again. We made a fire, one group boiled potato and another prepared dough for this tasty traditional food 😊 After having dinner together, we watched the sky and talked about different various things. Actually, it was a busy day, but I loved it.

On the fourth day, Iaroslav started to work on the wall’s constraction. Alejandro and I had breakfast and tidied up the room. Then I played with a cat for a while. I called it Fıstık (it means peanut in Turkish). And that’s was our last day in Stina. To be honest, before coming here I thought it would be a great opportunity to discover myself, meet locals and spend time with youngsters. But I had some prejudices about village life (not taking a shower, outdoor toilet and primitive life). But the truth is during these three days we managed to live well; we worked, cooked I mean we made things from scratch (vareniki) and more importantly learnt together. Bye for now. data.text: Opportunity: European Solidarity Corps "Poton Theatre"
Dates: October 2021 – October 2022 (12 months)
Location: Bátovce, Slovak Republic
Hosting Organization: Poton Theatre
About organization:
Pôtoň Theatre and Cultural Center operates in a small village of Bátovce - on a periphery. It is the only Slovak theatre located in countryside, 160 km from the capital of Slovakia - Bratislava.

Since 2019 Pôtoň holds Quality Label to act as hosting organization for the volunteering project under the auspices of the European Solidarity Corps. Pôtoň promotes and produces dance and theatre performances, audio-visual works, exhibitions and new media works.
It develops many projects focused on youth such as creative workshops, lectures, live libraries, non-formal educational projects and art therapy workshops
Pôtoň regularly offers its space for more than 50 professional contemporary artists each year within its residency programme.
Why volunteering with Pôtoň Theatre:

● gain new skills and knowledge and build experience for your future
● meet new people, artists and professionals from different fields and backgrounds and feel part of a team
● make a positive impact on someone’s live
● work on your own artistic/creative project with professional support of the team
● get to know the local community and give something back

The aim is to provide young people from Ukraine with the opportunity to take part in an creative a social projects of the Pôtoň center and to collaborate with the professional team, invited artists, guests and other volunteers on all the interesting projects on going in the center.
Who we are looking for

As a volunteer you will receive an introduction to the tasks and training for your role. You do not need any specific qualification or experience, but it's better if you are
● friendly and respectful to cultures that are different to your own
● art and culture interested / with artistic or technical background

● good listener willing to learn new skills
● helpful and empathetic

The main activity of volunteers is usually preparing and implementing workshops for kids. They work with children on different artistic projects (fine art, movement, dance, drama classes etc.), but they also help with all the tasks connected to the theatrical productions, lectures, performances. As it has been mentioned, the organsation provides residential stays for young artists, volunteers help them with their artistic projects too. All kinds of people are welcomed, not only those who are somehow related to the world of art, but also young people with some technical knowledge or interests, so they can assist in technical matters and learn a lot about this specific field within theatrical and artistic production.
Expenses
your travel expenses will be covered
your accommodation expenses will be covered
you will receive pocket money 5 EUR per day
you will receive daily allowance to cover your expenses on meals
Further benefits for you as a volunteer

● guidance and support during all your stay
● slovak SIM card

● all the coordination, trainings, mental and material support for your work for organisation and for your own creative project

Opportunity: European Solidarity Corps "Volunteer. More"
Dates: August 2021 – January 2022 (6 months)
Location: Kielce, Poland
Hosting Organization: Regionalne Centrum Wolontariatu
About the project

In the context of a European exchange, volunteers are needed to promote European values in a cultural and linguistic exchange program. They will be brought to share their culture and respective languages in active participation in community life. For this purpose, volunteering will take place in different institutions of cultural exchange in the city. Namely: The Cultural Center of Kielce, The Public Library, and Stanislaw Staszic Primary School No. 1.
The Organizers

The Regionalne Centrum Wolontariatu is an association that organizes socio-cultural activities, artistic and cultural events at a local and regional level but also hosting European volunteers since 2011. The trainers and coaches here cooperate with the School of Leaders, Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and the National Institute of Freedom. In the end, the Regional Volunteer Center is one of the most active NGOs in the region. The Association cooperates with institutions with various activities, as for example: cultural, caring, social, sports, student, ecological organizations and institutions As a result, it organizes and promotes events related to these areas and help to involve volunteers in local activities.
Main tasks

As a volunteer from the Europan solidarity Corps program, your role is to take an active part in the promotion of European values, civic activity, cultural diversity.
You will have to prepare exhibitions presenting interesting facts from your country. You will also have access to weekly Polish classes and be in contact with a mentor and other volunteers (2 hours a week) on-site to make this experience more enriching in the European sharing spirit.
Cultural Center (Kielce Centrum Kultury)

As a volunteer in this institution, you will have to promote and organize cultural events (concerts, performances, exhibitions, meetings with authors, educational and theatrical workshops), in accordance with the current schedule of events. You are going to take part at each step of the process: preparatory activities, the realization of the event and evaluation activities of individual events - in the KCK - service of stage facilities - care for foreign artists and guests, service of dressing
rooms, assistance with rehearsals, planning the stay associated with the performance, service of the audience of the Small and Large Stage.
• promotion of cultural events in Kielce Cultural Centre (promotion in social media, promotional trips to other organizations, distribution of promotional materials, working with a graphic designer creating promotional materials)
• assistance in organizing cultural education, artistic education, art education, theater classes with adult children and seniors (care of participants, assistance in organizing and conducting workshops),
• organization of exhibitions in the Gallery of Contemporary Art Elevator
• assistance in creating an English-speaking website of the Kielce Cultural Center

• assistance in the distribution of tickets for events organized
• animation of the education zone
Cultural center web site : https://www.kck.com.pl/
Library (Miejska Biblioteka Publiczna)

A pair of volunteers will:
• conduct language talks (based on books and magazines in the language library).

• support the cleaning work of librarians (take care of the order on the shelves with a foreign-language book collection, clean the shelves, arrange the book collection, preserves books).
• actively help in organizing cultural events, educational activities and reading animations.
• help in preparing promotional materials for the library.

• 3 hours - extra-curricular activities developing interests and talents, (1 hour of the "Single Notes" choir, 1 hour of the School of Nature "Curious of the World", 1 hour of the school circle artistic "Kredka" 1 hour of the School Circle of the League of Nature Protection, 1 hour of classes developing hobbies and interests of chess students,
• 3 hours of sports activities,

• 2 hours of dance workshops as part of the SKS extra-curricular activities,
• 9 hours - extra-curricular activities as part of psychological and pedagogical assistance

• 1 hour a week - classes in the school daycare center
• 4 hours a week as part of the School Volunteer Circle,

Additionally:

• 1 hour - classes with a school consultant, class planning and discussions

• 4 hours - preparing the exits, organizing tournaments, games and plays in the facility Volunteers will also cooperate with the Student Council and the Parents Council in organizing annual vacations, fairs, competitions, sports tournaments, and festivals.

ied for and approved. Please, be aware that individual kilometer distances might be further than allowed reimbursement. Travel costs will be reimbursed after receiving all documents from all participants. Meals will be provided with extra
